about: Forbidden lines in glowing gas (O4 part 1): how often electrons excite an ion's slow-to-shine level, and how far into the nebula each ion's zone reaches.

equation.name: How often electrons knock an ion into the state that gives a forbidden line
equation.formula:
m = 2 * pi * me
beta = h * h / sqrt(m * m * m * k * T)
q21 = beta * Y / g2
q12 = beta * Y / g1 * exp(-h * c / (lam * k * T))

T.name: temperature of the free electrons in the glowing gas

lam.name: the line's wavelength, which sets the energy each knock must give

Y.name: how readily an electron knock makes the jump, averaged over the electrons' speeds (effective collision strength)

g1.name: statistical weight of the lower level or term

g2.name: statistical weight of the upper level

q12.name: knocks up into the upper level, per ion per electron per cubic metre per second

q21.name: knocks back down without light, per ion per electron per cubic metre per second

source.text: Osterbrock, D. E. and Ferland, G. J. 2006, Astrophysics of Gaseous Nebulae and Active Galactic Nuclei

explain.curious: In a glowing nebula, fast electrons bump into oxygen and sulphur ions and lift them into states that can only shed their energy as light very slowly. On Earth a collision would steal it first; in a nebula's thin gas the light gets out, which is where the green of oxygen and the red of sulphur come from.
explain.science: Collisional excitation rate coefficient from a Maxwellian electron gas, with the thermally averaged collision strength; de-excitation by detailed balance.

equation.name: How much of the glowing gas a star's harder light reaches
equation.formula: f = if Qa <= 0 or a <= 0 then 0 else min(1, Qe / (a * Qa))

Qe.name: photons a second hard enough to make (or strip) this ion

Qa.name: ionising photons a second the nebula takes up (its recombinations)

a.name: atoms per hydrogen atom of the gas that takes these photons (1 for hydrogen, about a tenth for helium)

f.name: share of the glowing gas, nearest the star first, that those photons keep in this state

source.text: Osterbrock, D. E. and Ferland, G. J. 2006, Astrophysics of Gaseous Nebulae and Active Galactic Nuclei

explain.curious: Only a hot star's hardest light can strip oxygen twice, and that light is used up close in. So doubly ionised oxygen glows in the middle and sulphur, which needs less, glows near the edge: the reason nebula pictures have teal hearts and red rims.
explain.science: Photon counting: an ion's zone is the share of the ionised volume that the photons above its threshold can keep ionised. They are taken up by the gas whose edge lies just below them (hydrogen, or helium above 24.6 eV), which balances them with its own recombinations, so the zone scales as Q(>E) / (a Q_H).

explain.curious: An ion can only be stripped by a photon with enough energy, and it is easiest to hit just above that threshold. Harder photons slip past more often.
explain.science: Analytic fit to Opacity Project and Hartree-Dirac-Slater photoionisation cross-sections of the outer shell, valid from threshold to the next inner-shell edge.

equation.name: How an element splits between two ions where light strips and electrons rejoin
equation.formula: x = if al * ne <= 0 then 0 else 1 / (1 + G / (al * ne))

G.name: how often each ion of the lower kind is stripped by the starlight here

al.name: how readily the upper ion catches an electron back

x.name: share of the element left as the lower ion

source.text: Osterbrock, D. E. and Ferland, G. J. 2006, Astrophysics of Gaseous Nebulae and Active Galactic Nuclei

explain.curious: Starlight keeps stripping sulphur while electrons keep putting it back together. Close to the star the light wins; out near the edge, where the light is spread thin, the electrons win and once-ionised sulphur glows red.
explain.science: Ionisation equilibrium between adjacent stages: n(X+) Γ = n(X++) α nₑ.
